By integrating verification methods into Bayesian inference procedures, researchers aim to incorporate adversarial robustness into statistical analysis. A possible framework for achieving this involves reformulating the traditional Bayesian posterior distribution as a solution to the minimum of multiple functional values derived from data and hypothesis classes, resulting in a quantity that can be analytically verified within specified sets. Building on this concept, a characterization of verifiable posterior distributions is developed in relation to optimal transport theory, leading to a method for generating verified samples from these distributions. A specific implementation of this idea is explored in the context of regression analysis using a polyhedral hypothesis space, resulting in a computationally tractable method. Experimental findings confirm that this method generates verified predictions accurate up to a certain epsilon for a trained model even when subjected to inputs up to twice as far from the training set, achieving a balance between robustness and accuracy. In particular, it has been found that posterior contraction rates can influence verification stability, with certain rates making verification impossible within specified sets. It has also been determined that noise present in experimental data can prevent precise verification but does not affect the general approach to incorporating adversarial robustness into statistical analysis. Research remains to be done in broadening the approach to more complex models and incorporating complexity measures into the analysis. It has been suggested that studying verifiable distributions may provide insights into the inherent robustness properties of statistical models. It has also been noted that incorporating robustness into Bayesian inference could have practical applications in fields such as engineering and life sciences. Prior work on combining verification and inference procedures has concentrated on point estimators but has expanded to include other statistical tools in recent times. It now seems that the incorporation of verification into statistical analysis is an area of research that is growing rapidly and may offer novel insights into data. It is hypothesized that the generated verified samples could be utilized as a novel validation technique for training robust models. It is also speculated that future research may explore the incorporation of verification into statistical methods for estimating densities. To conclude, a promising area of research within the realm of adversarial machine learning has been identified in the rapidly evolving field of statistical analysis. It is possible that the distinctive features of verification analysis can offer novel perspectives and insights into data that were not previously explored within the context of adversarial robustness. This study investigates the effects of dimensionality reduction techniques on hyperspectral image classification. Spectral dimensionality reduction methods can efficiently process large datasets but might affect classification accuracy. We evaluated the performance of different methods, including principal component analysis, self-target component analysis, discrete wavelet transform, and random forest, using a synthetic dataset. Our findings show that PCA and STCA retain more detailed spectral information, resulting in better classification performance, particularly in accurately capturing features relevant to classification. Conversely, DWT was found to disrupt this capture, likely due to its approximation nature. Consequently, researchers should choose spectral dimensionality reduction methods carefully to avoid impacting hyperspectral image classification. Furthermore, this study highlights the importance of considering the inherent structure within data when selecting appropriate dimensionality reduction methods. We also provide guidance on the suitable applications and limitations of the methods evaluated. Notably, our study's conclusions align with existing theories on hyperspectral image classification, underscoring the value of theoretical frameworks in guiding real-world hyperspectral imaging tasks. Compressing large language models with new compression techniques has become increasingly viable, thanks to adjustable precision control in arithmetic units. This option allows models to be effectively compressed to a fraction of their original size, in proportion to the degree of precision reduction, without a corresponding scaling back of the input text complexity. We investigated the extent to which current large language models can be effectively compressed, particularly when we adjust the precision step by step (in increments of 0.25) and use the original text distribution as our reference point for evaluation. Our key findings reveal that when we apply the uniform averaging method for model weight compression and incrementally lower the precision, we can reduce the size of our models by four times, while only experiencing a slight deterioration in zero-shot learning outcomes. Notably, this compression has a minimal effect on the models' capacity to understand complex text and generate responses accordingly. We discovered that incremental precision reductions can lead to size reductions of up to ten times with only marginal impacts on zero-shot learning performance. We make our models and associated code open-source for the benefit of the community. A novel prediction method, referred to as ProCS, enables fast and precise calculation of crucial chemical shift indicators in proteins, thereby determining the 3D structure of proteins. ProCS uses quantum mechanical principles to predict the chemical shift of individual protein atoms, thereby confirming the accuracy of predicted structures. In a study involving over 14,000 protein residues from the Protein Data Bank, ProCS's reliability in predicting chemical shifts was assessed, and the results revealed a significant improvement in predicting certain chemical shift types with root mean square deviation values below 0.5 parts per million. ProCS has been successfully used to verify and refine protein structures at a large scale, and the method has been incorporated into the PHAISTOS protein structure prediction pipeline. Furthermore, ProCS has the potential to significantly contribute to the verification and refinement of protein structures, thereby advancing our understanding of protein function and its relationship with disease. The choice of loss function plays a crucial role in the training of neural networks, yet there's a lack of research on how different loss functions affect the generalizability of the model. Our study aimed to investigate the impact of loss function selection, and we found that using a combination of methods can provide superior performance to using a single loss function. Furthermore, we discovered that utilizing an ensemble of loss functions in training leads to improved testing accuracy and reduced overfitting. Notably, our experiments involved widely used classification datasets, and we observed consistent outcomes regardless of the dataset's size. Additionally, we analyzed the effect of loss function variation at the feature level and found that using an ensemble of loss functions can provide more accurate predictions for out-of-distribution data. Our findings suggest that incorporating multiple loss functions has the potential to enhance the robustness and reliability of neural networks, particularly when dealing with uncertain data. The process of exciton condensation leads to the spontaneous creation of electron-hole pairs and triggers a phase transition in a semimetal that forms an excitonic insulator by creating a gap at the Fermi surface. This theoretical concept has been around for decades, but current methods only allow for the evaluation of excitonic effects within a simplified framework. Using an ab initio technique that incorporates no assumptions beyond what is provided in the density functional theory, researchers have developed a corresponding perturbation theory. Applying this approach to the material TiSe2, which is known to undergo an excitonic phase transition, yielded results that agree with experimental x-ray spectroscopy. The technique has been validated as a reliable tool for studying exciton condensation in materials that are candidate excitonic insulators. Further analysis using this approach has revealed that the excitonic phase in TiSe2 is actually unstable in a free-electron environment, but becomes stable when considering its actual lattice. Conversely, results suggest that the lattice itself is not primarily responsible for the excitonic phase transition in TiSe2. These findings mark an important breakthrough in the study of exciton condensation and may pave the way for the identification of other potential excitonic insulators. Additionally, the developed technique has the potential to contribute to our broader understanding of quantum many-body systems, including the potential creation of new materials with unique properties through the stabilization of exotic phases. Lastly, the technique has laid the groundwork for the examination of exciton condensation in other two-dimensional materials, with candidate materials including strantitanide and TaS2. Finally, the calculated gap sizes in these materials, including TaS2 and TaSe2, demonstrate a considerable variation that could be addressed in future research. The underlying software code employed in this study has been publicly released for others to build upon. Specifically, the code used in this research is an extension of the Open Source Phillybeans/CP2K package, with the modifications and new code specifically related to the research being shared under the Apache2 License at the physeics.seaberry GitHub repository. We introduce a new paradigm for computer security called "minimax engaged learning," where both the learner and attacker exchange roles to form recurring cycles of training and adversarial testing. Initial experiments using this approach with support vector machines in adversarial networks reveal a notable shift in the balance of power from the learner to the adversary. Notably, as the number of data points available for training increases, the performance gap between the learner and adversary decreases, albeit with the latter maintaining a steady advantage. Our analysis also indicates that utilizing the adversary's knowledge to update the training data can improve the learner's resilience, ultimately benefiting both the learner and adversary in subsequent adversarial tests. Our findings highlight both the benefits and limitations of the minimax engaged learning framework, prompting the need for further research into its potential applications and practical implementations. The purpose of this research is to explore how music has changed over time in terms of its underlying mathematical structure. We calculated the statistical properties of song lyrics and song meanings from the SongNet dataset to represent their intellectual content. We discovered that, quantitatively, the content of Western music has become more intricate and alluring throughout history, spanning from the Middle Ages to the present. We compare the developmental trajectory of musical content with the developmental trajectory of literary work, revealing both similarities and differences. We also find that the shifts in musical content are correlated with the shifts in the social environment of that period. We speculate that these modifications are the result of two fundamental forces driving creative progress: the pursuit of artistic originality and the influence of the environment. We hope that our study encourages more discussions about the intricate connection between music, culture, and cognition. We also provide a mathematical framework that can be used to study the intricate content of music and other artistic forms. This research has the potential to significantly advance our comprehension of the intricate nature of art and its significance in both creative processes and social environments. Ludics is a mathematical framework for concurrent interaction, also serving as a proof theory. It was initially developed as a standalone concept but has a underlying connection to linear logic. We will demonstrate that its behavioral semantics is equivalent to a domain with specific structural rules, similar to Girard's games semantics. This connection is rooted in the harmonic interpretation, an embedding of the ludics proof structure into games. Furthermore, we highlight that the structural rules in question have a direct correlation with the concepts of continuity and algebraicity, leading to a realization that the harmonic interpretation serves as a form of denotational semantics. This understanding can be seen as a variant of the Curry-Howard correspondence, where a proof structure is translated into a domain, and subsequently, a meaning interpretation is applied to it. This insight also enables a relationship between notions of correctness in ludics and continuity, making it a form of proof irreducibility. Since ludics can be seen as a form of proof, we explore how this insight relates to Brouwerian intuitionism. Ultimately, we conclude with an observation of a parallel between the notion of harmonicity and Brouwerian intuitionistic negation, leading to a possibility that an extension of the ludics framework could serve as an intuitive framework for Brouwerian intuitionistic logic. A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to rank compiled datasets more efficiently, as we demonstrate a feasible way to aggregate comparisons via unsupervised clustering techniques. Although the resulting grouped comparisons introduce classification ambiguity regarding which comparisons to prioritize, we show that these challenges can be resolved using basic distanced-based methods. To evaluate the practical usefulness of our approach, we developed interactive tools that enable human labeling and facilitate real-time monitoring of the learning process. Our proposal allows for learning rewards with reduced labeling expenses of up to 24.6x compared to individual comparisons, using the same number of labels. Moreover, our framework yields greater stability and consistently adapts more quickly to changing rewards compared to prior reward learning methods. This study reveals the occurrence of closed vortices in two-dimensional ideal fluids, comprising three types: geometric, logarithmic, and hyperbolic. The research demonstrates that these vortices can exist for limited periods, forming seamless, non-interacting pairs. The experiments show that external disturbances can make the vortices unstable and cause them to dissipate at a constant rate, independent of the intensity of the disturbance. The rate of dissipation is found to be consistent with theoretical predictions from nonlinear wave theory, providing new insights into the behavior of two-dimensional ideal fluids. The research also validates a previously proposed wave model, showing that it accurately captures the significant features of the fluid's behavior. The study confirms that this model is valid at low Keenans numbers and for very long periods of time, but finds that high-intensity external disturbances cause the model to fail due to the loss of the fluid's underlying integrability. The research offers a statistical explanation for this failure, providing a new perspective on the spatial and temporal development of two-dimensional turbulence. The study finds that the temporal development of the turbulence follows a power-law pattern and discovers a previously unexplained exponent in the process. The research also makes an unexpected connection between the fluctuations in the fluid's energy and the distribution of its vorticities, revealing a deep similarity between the two. The study provides a statistical understanding of this similarity and shows that it holds across a wide range of conditions. The research also reveals a hidden connection between the fluctuations in the fluid's energy and the characteristics of its hyperbolic vortices, unlocking a long-standing puzzle in the field. The study finds that the power-law pattern observed in the fluid's energy and the distribution of its vortices is not unique to the occurrents, but rather a feature shared by a wide range of non-trivial systems, including the occurrents and other two-dimensional fluids. The research offers a new statistical approach to identifying power-law distributions and provides a series of prescriptions for doing so, including a novel statistical method known as the cumulative distribution function inverse. The study finds that the power-law pattern observed in the fluid's energy and the distribution of its vortices is robust to a variety of underlying structures, including the Occurrents and a non-occurrent two-dimensional fluid governed by a hyperbolic metric. The research also reveals a deep connection between the patterns observed in the fluid's energy and the distribution of its vortices, showing that they are closely linked and providing a new statistical approach for studying this relationship

A significant challenge in addressing unbalanced data in surveys and analyses is known as selection bias, which threatens the validity of inferences. The Aim of Probability Weighting (APW) is an efficient method for reducing selection bias by weighting observations based on predicted probabilities. However, this approach can be limited by the accuracy of probability predictions and the complexity of the weighting scheme. Improving the efficiency of APW while accounting for the uncertainty in probability predictions has become a pressing issue. In this study, a modified Standardized APW procedure (SAPW) is developed to enhance the efficiency of APW by scaling observations using predicted probabilities from a neural network. SAPW's parametric assumption about the conditional mean model helps reduce the influence of noisy probability predictions when calculating the APW weight. As a result, this method achieves better efficiency compared to traditional APW when working with parametric models for the mean. SAPW's efficiency can also be further improved by leveraging neighboring observations. Two main benefits of SAPW weights are that they are orthogonal to the sample mean and covariance, which helps maintain robustness to outliers and generates interpretable inference results. Our approach provides a solution to a critical research question in the field of survey statistics and imputation techniques, and its efficiency and accuracy are substantiated through simulations and real-world data analysis. Additionally, the underlying code used in this study has been made available for reference. Structural equation modeling with balanced and biased data is another area of interest covered in this report, as well as an assessment of SAPW's performance across diverse data sets. Finally, recommendations for practicing researchers have been provided, encompassing guidelines for implementing the SAPW procedure in real-world data analysis. A key recommendation involves the utilization of SAPW weights in model estimation when a parametric mean model is applied. Also, specific guidelines for the choice of bandwidth in local smoothing have been offered. Finally, general advice on the use of SAPW weights has been provided to researchers. The combination of experimental findings from the LHCb, Belle, and Belle II collaborations provides a precise prediction of the Cabbibo angle and heavy quark masses, which serves as a strong test of the standard model's accuracy. However, there are discrepancies found between the predicted and observed results, particularly in the relationship between the CP-violating angle $\beta$ and $\Delta M_K$, the mass difference between the kaon's ground and first excited states, which presents a significant area of inquiry for future investigation. Advancements in the understanding of $\beta$ and $\beta_s$ in $\tau$ decays as well as $\tau$ decays into hadronic parts will significantly contribute to the estimation of the hadronic part of the muon's magnetic moment and make the $\tau$-factor an essential element in the solution of the hadronic part of the muon's anomaly. This hadronic part is anticipated to be understood with an accuracy of 0.5 MeV/c^2 by the time the LHC reaches its design luminosity. The development of theory close to this precision of 0.3 MeV/c^2 for the $\tau$-decay into light leptons and very low mass mesons will be essential. This precision is also essential for the estimation of the $\tau$ mass, which will be possible with an accuracy of 0.2 MeV/c^2 thanks to the $\tau$-factor and radio-frequency corrections implemented in the Belle II detector. Additionally, the precision needed for the $\tau$-decays into hadrons and $\beta_s$ will stimulate the enhancement of the lattice QCD precision to the level of 20 MeV/c^2 in the light quark masses and to the level of 30 MeCH^3/dx in the light quark mass splitting. The development of the required theoretical precision over the next decade will be crucial and will be driven by the tension between the predicted and observed precision seen currently. The necessary precision will be achieved through a collaborative effort involving particle theory, lattice QCD, and experiment, driven by the need to resolve the anomalies in the $\tau$ and $K$ physics. This collective effort will be the key to understanding whether the observed discrepancies can be explained within the framework of the SM or if these anomalies could be hints at the existence of beyond the SM physics. The next decade will be dedicated to resolving these questions, which will be answered only through a collaborative and precise investigation of the $\tau$ and $K$ physics

This study examines the variability of baroclinic waves in a rotating, buoyancy-driven flow within a cylindrical container. The scenario is akin to a simplified atmospheric mesoscale in mid-latitude regions. A comprehensive experimental research was conducted using a large-scale apparatus, comprising 4.5 meters in height and 3.5 meters in width, to investigate the inherent unpredictability in this system. The findings from these experiments were then compared with numerical simulations performed using a state-of-the-art climate model. The goals of this study include evaluating the inherent uncertainties associated with this system and appraising the abilities of high-resolution numerical models in capturing the complexities of geophysical flows. The comparison between the two methodologies also sheds light on how uncertainties influence the simulation of these complex systems. A typical strategy for modeling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-independent extreme value parameters, it comes with the challenge of difficult parameter estimation. We propose a new approach to ease this difficulty by linking the parameters of the Poisson process with those of a parametric extreme value distribution. This technique relies on the relationship between the parameters and the mean excess function over a range of thresholds, rather than just a single threshold, as in traditional methods. We demonstrate that our approach makes it feasible to perform efficient maximum likelihood estimation of the extreme value parameters when the Poisson process parameters are known. We also derive expressions for the asymptotic covariance matrix and a consistency measure, which enables us to evaluate the accuracy of estimators. We introduce a way to compare estimators based on a lack-of-fit measure, leading to the discovery of underbias in this context, indicating that estimators tend to perform better than expected. We show the results of simulations illustrating the accuracy of the proposed estimators and validate them using real-world data sets. The findings indicate that our approach offers a reliable solution for the reliable estimation of extreme value parameters in the framework of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. corruption. Our framework ensures that the estimated policy remains close to

can be obtained without first finding a solution under the standard assumption

policy estimation, but we anticipate it will be generalizable to a broader

limits of robustness and provide empirical evidence of the trade-offs between

A new, more efficient algorithm has been devised for $N\times N$ matrices, enabling faster calculation of the generalized convolutions at an complexity cost of $O(N^2 \log^2 N)$. In this additional analysis, we find that the efficiency of the parallel implementation depends on the size of the matrices, specifically that the $O(N^2 \log N)$ cost can be achieved in a sufficient number of iterations with a sufficiently large matrix size. These quantities, related to $CP$ violation in $B_s^0$ decays, are essential for completing the standard model and are the focus of ongoing research at the LHCb experiment. The advantages and challenges of predicting these values using QCD-based methods and the potential for determining them experimentally within the next few years are examined. Specifically, the report outlines the current status of predictions for $\phi_s^{\rm PSK}$ and $\Delta\Gamma_s$ derived from the perturbative QCD method at the tree level, the importance of including decay-by-decay width correlations and indirect decays in predictions for $\phi_s^{\rm PSK}$ and $\Delta\Gamma_s$, and the anticipated uncertainties associated with these predictions. It also discusses the prospects for measuring these quantities at LHCb using semileptonic and non-leptonic decays, particularly $\beta_s$ and $\lambda_s$, and the expected precision, which is estimated to reach 0.0005 for $\phi_s^{\rm PSK}$ and 0.0001 for $\Delta\Gamma_s$ in 2012. Furthermore, the report considers the potential for improving these quantities by analyzing decay chains of heavy mesons, the likely limitations of this approach, and the expected effects of input parameters on the predictions for $\phi_s^{\rm PSK}$ and $\Delta\Gamma_s$. Finally, the report outlines areas for further study and presents a plan for a comprehensive theoretical analysis of $\phi_s^{\rm PSK}$ and $\Delta\Gamma_s$ in the near future. We demonstrate that, contrary to expectations, none of these methods can reliably detect changes in the Hamiltonian's polynomial degree. We also introduce a new method of analyzing operator growth and investigate its potential for generating a quantum advantage in simulating the Ising model. Utilizing a 400 ms beam, Hoyle state decays were measured over the interval 0-600 ns following creation. Demonstrating direct decay is evident up to 200 ns, and an analysis of proton-proton energy distributions reveals a distinct, isotropic component at an energy of approximately 743 keV. By "distant," I'm referring to horizontal distances that exceed the thickness of the aquifer. They're based on assumptions outlined below, followed by a step-by-step mathematical derivation in Appendix A.

Assumptions:

  1. Groundwater flow is steady-state.
  2. The flow system is confined.
  3. The horizontal extent of the aquifer is negligible compared to the vertical thickness.
  4. There's no vertical flow within the aquifer.
  5. There's a single head boundary at the aquitard layer above the aquifer and another at the aquitard layer at the bottom of the aquifer.

Starting with Darcy's Law for a comprehensive approach, we apply mass conservation principles to arrive at Darcy's Law for an individual element, then combine the results to establish a partial differential equation describing groundwater flow. This involves leveraging the simplified assumptions to consolidate the equations into a single equation for the horizontal groundwater velocity, which is accompanied by two ordinary differential equations describing the vertical gradient of potentiometric head and flow rate. Additionally, we derive four first-order partial differential equations that govern potentiometric head and flow rate under specific boundary conditions, which are validated through comparison with existing equations in the literature. Furthermore, we explore numerical examples to illustrate the application and evolution of potentiometric head over time across varying distances from the initial head boundary. Lastly, Darcy's Law is validated for an individual element under specific conditions. Please refer to Appendix A for detailed mathematical derivations. 

It's worth noting that these equations are intended for use in scenarios involving groundwater flow over relatively long distances and are most suitable for confined aquifers with head boundary conditions at aquitard layers above and below the aquifer. They're also best applied when the horizontal extent of the aquifer doesn't significantly affect its thickness. Additionally, they're not specifically designed for scenarios involving recharge or discharge at the water table or shallow, uncompacted aquifers. For such cases, the equations would require modification through additional mathematical derivations, which are not included here.

Machine learning models typically assume data labels are certain, but in reality, they can be ambiguous, incomplete, or unreliable. This project introduces a novel learning paradigm, based on argumentation theory, to handle quantified uncertainty in data labels. By formulating decision-making processes using tree-like structures, called Indecision Trees, this study develops a corresponding algorithm and demonstrates its application on two benchmark problems. Compared to traditional approaches, InDTree excels at learning under complete uncertainty, while its general version can learn even when data labels are uncertain, incomplete, or unreliable, albeit at a computational cost. A related framework, called Indecision Forests, is also introduced to improve model robustness and scalability. Further research will investigate the adoption of other argumentation techniques to enhance machine learning's handling of uncertainty. However, its original time complexity still falls short for dealing with very large datasets, particularly when using DTW's non-linear nature. Building on PrunedDTW, Early Discarding PrunedDTW (EDPDTW) addresses these issues by incorporating two innovations: firstly, it enhances PrunedDTW's linearization process to achieve optimal results; secondly, it introduces an early discarding strategy, thus reducing the number of candidate sequences considered in the search. EDPTW surpasses PrunedDTW in efficiency and accuracy, yielding a linear time complexity that is independent of the sequence length for similarity searches. EDPTW also outperforms other optimized approaches, such as SpiralDTW and SADTW, by a significant margin. Moreover, our approach accurately captures the underlying nonlinear pattern present in sign language videos, ultimately reflecting the inherent nature of similarity-based PrunedDTW. Current educational tools used in testing can either provide coverage insights comparable to professional tools or highlight instructor-set testing priorities, but not both. As a result, instructors are faced with a choice: train students using industry-standard testing methods, thereby equipping them with valuable skills, but potentially limiting their understanding of testing objectives, or, demonstrate testing objectives through tailored insights, enriching students' knowledge, but lacking real-world relevance. This study sought to address this concern by introducing two types of educational testing environments: the testing education system (TES) and the prioritized testing education system (PTES). TES mimics professional tool feedback, while PTES allows instructors to set testing priorities, providing unique insights to students. This study analyzed the effect of employing PTES or TES on two sets of testing courses: one comprised of basic exercises and another with more advanced projects. Student performance, feedback, and learning experiences were evaluated when using either the TES or PTES method. Data indicated that using PTES yielded better grades and more extensive code coverage compared to using TES. Additionally, instructor and student feedback, as well as project completion rates, were superior when PTES was employed. It appears that prioritizing testing objectives through PTES provides an effective balance between equipping students with valuable testing skills and ensuring they grasp the practical aspects of testing objectives. Prioritizing testing education comes with recommendations to instructors on how to effectively utilize PTES in their teaching practices. Instructors can leverage PTES as a tool to guide students in selecting testing methods and emphasizing areas that require additional testing, while also incorporating industry-standard testing practices through TES. By combining the strengths of both TES and PTES, a well-rounded educational testing environment can be established, equipping students with real-world testing skills and providing a practical understanding of testing objectives essential for successful software testing. In tasks involving safety-sensitive systems, decisions made by machine learning models can be difficult for users to understand. With the advent of neural networks, which operate by translating inputs into high-dimensional feature spaces, explaining these decisions has become even more complicated. Although various methods exist to clarify model decisions, few have been successful in translating these explanations into knowledge that can be legally actioned. To address this issue, we've developed a new approach, called ExplainNN, which uses a concept analysis technique within a machine learning framework to break down decisions made by neural networks into more manageable ILP (Integer Linear Programming) components. By employing a concept analysis technique to identify key features characterised by human expertise, ExplainNN reduces the complexity of model decisions to a set of features that can be legally acted upon, making it easier for users to understand the decisions made by neural networks. Based on experiments using datasets from the healthcare and finance industries, ExplainNN outperformed other methods in accurately translating model explanations into knowledge that can be legally actioned. For example, when testing the model on a dataset from the healthcare industry, ExplainNN achieved a recall of 97.8% for translating model explanations into knowledge that can be legally actioned. With its potential to simplify decision-making processes across a range of fields, ExplainNN could be an important tool for many industries seeking to understand and work with the decisions made by neural networks. While incorporating human expertise into the model explanations, ExplainNN also demonstrates how neural networks trained on industry-specific datasets can be used to generate summaries of legal contracts and memoranda. Additionally, ExplainNN provides a range of features that can be used as inputs in subsequent ILP models, effectively capturing the decision-making logic employed by neural networks. Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) are widely used for node classification in
undirected graphs. However, these models face difficulties in handling large
graphs due to their implicit graph down-sampling method, which neglects graph
details. Recent improvements, such as Graph Attention Networks (GATs), address this
issue but still suffer from an 'over-blurring' effect, diminishing graph features
in the prediction outcome. This problem is not seen in models like Neural Networks
(NNs), which treat input data as general features rather than graph-related data.
We compared GCNs and GATs with NNs and found significant differences in
performance, particularly on datasets with distinct cluster structures. These
results suggest that models like GCNs and GATs are better suited for tasks relying
on well-defined graph features and are preferred over NNs. Furthermore, we found
that re-training models on enlarged graphs (e.g., doubling the nodes) does not
necessarily improve performance, highlighting their limitations in capturing
global graph properties. This study confirms the 'over-blurring' effect of GCNs and
GATs and provides empirical evidence to guide model selection for node
classification based on graph characteristics. The code for this research is
available at https://github.com/abhishekshambhu/Over-blurring_effect_of_GCNs.

Internet Service Providers (ISPs) have long expected users to bear data expenses,
despite users now being able to purchase unlimited plans from these same ISPs.
Content Providers, on the other hand, typically only compensate ISPs for data
transfers when users access their content via streaming or downloading.
Notably, standard data transfer fees do not adequately compensate ISPs for the
bandwidth consumed when users stream high-definition content.
To address this disconnect, this research proposes a model in which Content
Providers contractually agree to compensate ISPs for the bandwidth consumed
during these streaming activities.
A key challenge in implementing this model lies in determining fair pricing for
bandwidth, as well as Content Provider allocations, given the complexities and
variations in users' streaming habits.
To this end, this research develops a mathematical framework for addressing these
issues, demonstrated through numerical analyses and decision-making scenarios.  Crucially, this model differs from traditional revenue sharing models, as it is
based on the actual data consumption resulting from user content access.  Furthermore,
this research highlights content-specific factors that could potentially influence
bandwidth pricing and Content Provider allocations.  Through simulations, this data
is utilized to derive pricing and allocation values for the ISP and Content
Providers, respectively.  Notably, these values are shown to be dependent on
variances in user content consumption.  Specifically, this research indicates that
the ISP and Content Providers benefit equally under the QRE equilibrium when
streaming rates are homogeneous, but the disparity in their returns grows as the
variance in user content consumption increases.  These results can be attributed
to the corresponding increase in the valuations for content, resulting in
differing return distributions.  Ultimately, this research yields a valuable
insight, as it enables Content Providers to determine whether an ISP will unfairly
benefit from data transfer fees at the expense of these Providers' profits.  In
particular, these results indicate that the difference in returns between the ISP
and Content Providers is positively correlated with the variances in user content
consumption, as well as the corresponding valuations for content.  Conversely, it
is observed that the ISP and Content Providers are equally benefited when streaming
rates are homogeneous, as their returns display symmetry.  Building upon
initial research by Ho and Wellman, this study extends their findings, as it
assumes that Content Providers compensate the ISP for data consumption on a
per-user basis, as opposed to the aggregate bandwidth consumption assumed in

Subsequently, we employ our method to generate predictive distributions of cross-sectional average returns in two specific settings: one based on a capital asset pricing model and another on a modified version of the Fama-French model. Our results, which are derived analytically, reveal the influence of portfolio characteristics on the distribution of cross-sectional average returns and highlight the significance of considering both mean and variance properties in cross-sectional analysis. Furthermore, we illustrate the practical utility of our approach by using it to forecast the predictive distribution of average returns on the Fama-French portfolio tiers. This study evaluates the trustworthiness of bidders in second-price auctions through an experimental investigation. Trustworthiness is defined as the tendency to honor one's auction promise. Bidders may prioritize either fairness or their own financial gain when auctions fall through due to a withdrawal, and we investigate these scenarios. We consider a first withdrawal scenario, in which the auction winner receives zero payment, and a second, co-winner withdrawal scenario, in which payment is split equally. Bidders may feel unfairly treated in both situations but are only affected personally in the first case. Our experiment includes both a real-payout and a token-payout component, and prior to conducting the study, we developed a survey to gauge bidders' anticipated behavior. Our findings show that bidders tend to honor their auction promise in both withdrawal situations, but tend to depart from this commitment when payments are split equally. A comparison with predicted values indicates that bidders tend to place a higher value on fairness than the average predicted value. The results also show that bidders who participate in the first withdrawal scenario tend to honor their auction promise more frequently when payments are made at the auction's specified value rather than when payments are split equally. Interestingly, when auctions fall through due to a withdrawal, bidders who prefer higher payouts tend to depart from this commitment more frequently in the first withdrawal scenario, but tend to honor their auction promise more frequently in the second withdrawal scenario. Finally, when payments are made at the auction's specified value, bidders who prefer higher payouts tend to depart from this commitment more frequently in both withdrawal situations. To facilitate an understanding of these complex findings, we suggest considering a model in which bidders weigh fairness against their financial self-interest when making predictions about trustworthiness. Our study contributes to the existing body of auction-related research, particularly in the areas of second-price auctions, withdrawal scenarios, and the evaluation of trustworthiness. To create an effective ADHD diagnosis using Deep Learning, it is crucial to identify the essential brain regions associated with the disorder. We conducted a study to determine which regions of interest (ROIs) are essential for training a model to differentiate between ADHD and control individuals using resting-state functional MRI data. We compared three approaches to selecting essential regions: a forward feature selection method, a mutual information-based method, and an information gain-based method. We evaluated these approaches by training models on subsets of ROI data and assessed their performance using accuracy, AUC, and F1-score metrics. Based on our results, the mutual information-based method consistently provided the best performance and chose a common set of regions that are commonly linked to ADHD, including the default mode network and regions responsible for executive function. We found that including the selected essential regions in the model improved its accuracy by at least 5% compared to training on the full set of ROI data. Additionally, our study demonstrated that using a simple linear model achieved comparable performance to deep learning methods in diagnosing ADHD from fMRI data, highlighting the potential benefits of using shallow models for this task. Our code is available for reproduction of the study at https://github.com/pauldhar/ADHD_diagnosis_rsfMRI. Keywords: ADHD, rs-fMRI, deep learning, essential components, diagnostic performance. Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found in legal documents, technical reports, research papers, and other written content. While they facilitate quicker writing and communication, they can also introduce ambiguity if not properly defined or if their meanings shift over time. To enhance understanding, it is crucial to identify and clarify the meanings of acronyms and abbreviations within content, particularly in fields like Law and Medicine. MadDog is a web-based platform designed to support acronym detection and disambiguation across various domains and contexts. Utilizing an advanced tokenizer that accounts for punctuation, the platform identifies acronyms based on specific sentence structures and domain-specific dictionaries that define and differentiate the meanings of similar acronyms. MadDog provides pre-defined dictionaries for standard domains and allows users to create custom dictionaries for specialized fields, empowering users to take advantage of the platform's features in any acronym-rich domain. With its user-friendly interface, MadDog enables users to upload content in various formats (text, HTML, or URL) and obtain results in the original format with annotated acronyms linked to their definitions. Furthermore, the platform includes a search feature for dictionary management and acronym disambiguation. MadDog aims to facilitate understanding and comprehension within content by identifying and explaining the meanings of acronyms and abbreviations. With its comprehensive tools and customizability options, the platform aims to improve understanding and accuracy in tasks involving acronyms and abbreviations. In oscillatory media, regions that vibrate at a steady frequency can serve as pacemakers, syncing and sending waves through the medium at a constant speed. This process under ideal conditions leads to uniform, evenly spaced generations of waves. However, real-world factors often cause deviations in this mechanism, resulting in irregularities. Nonetheless, it's observable that, under certain circumstances, the pacemaker's effect can still be accurately modeled. Researchers have derived mathematical formulas for the speed at which waves propagate in two specific scenarios involving oscillatory motion: when the pacemaker oscillates at a frequency higher than the system's eigenfrequency, and when it's lower, but still affects the system's transient behavior. Our first approach, an adaptive NE estimator, employs a subsample of $m$ measurements from a quantum state $\rho$ and produces an NE estimate within a confidence interval $\pm \delta$. Both the interval width and the number of sampled states $m$ can be set in advance; this algorithm guarantees that the estimated range of NE will not exceed itself in subsequent runs. A prominent area of study in NISQ-era quantum computing involves exploring the potential for quantum computers to excel at machine learning, particularly when dealing with large datasets and complex problems. A key area within this field is quantum unsupervised learning - using quantum methods to analyze and identify patterns in data when little to no labels are provided. Another key area is guided learning, which uses quantum computers to efficiently execute tasks with limited supervision. However, there has been limited experimental investigation of these areas on superconducting quantum processors. This study addresses this gap by providing the first thorough examination of quantum unsupervised and guided learning on superconducting quantum processors. By analyzing various circuits and implementing them on IBM's 5-qubit quantum simulator, we evaluated the performance and variability of these algorithms. Our results indicate that the average variability of the estimated learning boundary in unsupervised tasks ranges from 1.5 to 3.5, and the average runtime in guided learning experiments ranges from 40-97 nanoseconds. Additionally, we found that guided learning can significantly outperform classical methods in certain tasks, executing them 1-2 orders of magnitude faster on average. These findings not only provide insight into the capabilities and reliability of quantum algorithms but also reveal potential avenues for future quantum computing applications. To address this need, we present Lotse, a practical approach for implementing guidance systems within visualizations. Historically, the stellarator's design has depended heavily on computational simulations aimed at minimizing its overall magnetic field structure's ellipticity and other inherent weaknesses. Recent breakthroughs involving novel magnetic surface coordinates and advanced data analysis techniques, specifically designed to optimize stellarator design, inspired the development of a new approach outlined below.

A new method utilizes these improved analytical tools to identify the most efficient stellarator design, one that not only reduces weaknesses like ellipticity but also enhances performance, achieving a level of optimization previously unattainable with traditional designs. This approach can be adapted for various magnetic configurations and, given the steady advancements in coordinate development and data analysis methods, is poised to revolutionize stellarator design, potentially leading to a future breakthrough in this field. A comprehensive dataset containing over 3,000 stellarator designs, thoroughly evaluated in terms of their efficiency, is made freely available at https://github.com/graflis/stellarator-samples. This research was made possible through a grant from the National Science Foundation, while a grant from the U.S. Department of Energy supported the associated computational simulations. Furthermore, this research benefited from a collaboration involving researchers from the U.S., Germany, and Italy, facilitated by the International Stellarator Collaboration. Additionally, the data described in this paper was made available through multiple public repositories, specifically arXiv (arXiv.2107.01430), GitHub (https://github.com/graflis/stellarator-samples), and DSM-CD (https://dx.doi.org/10.17632/4xdk6z5y9f24901798d0b0da9). A study used magnetic resonance imaging to observe temperature distribution within a horizontal tube filled with small glass beads while air flow was established using Peclet numbers ranging from 1 to  125. As flow accelerated, the typical gradient of temperature decreased and the distribution became more uniform, exhibiting symmetry despite the uneven air flow. The observed temperature distribution was also analyzed in relation to the air Prandelt number and found to deviate from theoretical predictions due to thermal conduction in the solid material. The time required to achieve stable temperature distribution decreased with increasing Peclet numbers, typically taking around five to six times the convection time to become nearly uniform. It's worth noting that the observed temperature variations were relatively small and the system achieved a quasi-steady state where the mean temperature and flow pattern didn't change significantly. The research provides visual representation of temperature arrangement within gas-solid systems, essential knowledge for understanding and modeling such systems. The research also offers a method for quantifying temperature variation and could be applied to study mass transfer in similar setups by replacing air with a suitable solution. The findings can influence the design of gas-solid contacts to enhance heat exchange and possibly promote uniform growth in crystallization processes. The research also highlights the potential and limitations of using MRI thermal imaging. The research used 1.5T MRI scanner to acquire 10 to 30 image slices with a resolution of around 0.7 mm while taking around 25-40 seconds per scan. Although this made synchronizing air flow challenging, the study demonstrated the feasibility of using MRI thermal imaging with low to medium air flow rates. Due to its capabilities and limitations, this technique can be used for future research on temperature distribution in various gas-solid systems, particularly with higher flow rates. Moreover, replacing air with a suitable solution could enable the study of mass transfer in gas-solid systems using this technique. A widespread occurrence in nature, aggregate formation involving multiple types of molecules is seen across plant, animal, and fungal life, often taking various shapes such as rings, spirals, and clusters. Research in physics, chemistry, and biology agrees that aggregates are composed of repeating units held together by intermolecular forces, but the field is lacking a unified mathematical approach to describe and simulate these structures accurately. This paper presents a novel mathematical framework that is versatile, efficient, and accurate in modeling diverse aggregate shapes and their dynamics. This framework also identifies specific parameters essential for conferring stability to aggregates through competition between intramolecular and extracellular forces. Simulation outcomes for multiple systems match real-world observations, thereby validating the proposed approach. Furthermore, this study demonstrates how the proposed mathematical model can be used to make predictions about aggregate behavior under varying environmental conditions. These predictions could be useful in understanding how external factors might affect bacterial curving and tumor cell aggregation, for example. This mathematical model, being the first of its kind, holds potential applications in predicting outcomes and informing decisions in biomedical fields such as cancer, infectious diseases, and biofilms. Finally, the paper highlights the benefits and variations of which closure approximation can be applied, offering possible avenues for further inquiry in applied mathematics, biomolecular modeling, and theoretical biophysics. Overall, this research lays the foundation for a comprehensive mathematical understanding of aggregate structures and their behaviors, extending beyond current models that might seem simple but are effective in informing clinical choices. This study aims to develop a fundamental, continuous mathematical model of aggregate structures and their dynamics, making it possible to study their movements and behaviors over extended periods, for instance, how bacteria move in a liquid environment. This distinction enables the proposed mathematical model to capture essential aspects of aggregate dynamics, such as their responsiveness to external stimuli and their ability to form complex shapes, which simpler models often lack. Additionally, this paper explores the limitations and possibilities of approximating aggregate distributions using continuous mathematical models and proposes a novel approach for dealing with aggregate dynamics using discrete mathematical models called "Potts models". These Potts models, originally used for studying particle interactions, are shown to be suitable for modeling aggregate structures and their shared components, thereby providing a potential solution to previously simple models in biomolecular research. Using daily SOHO/MIIPS data, the rotational movements and magnetic disruptions associated with flare activity in NOAA AR 11429 were studied. This research focused on monitoring the movements and magnetic changes of sunspots in NOAA AR 11429 over six consecutive days. On the day the region rotated off the disk, a significant magnetic disruption was observed, accompanied by major changes in the sunspot's magnetic field. These findings are in line with observations from other sources, indicating that NOAA AR 11429 underwent a full rotation within a time frame of approximately 48 hours before disappearing from the disk. Upon rotation, the region displayed characteristics reminiscent of a delta-sigma configuration, suggesting that instability and activity were heightened. Additionally, the region exhibited considerable magnetic disturbances prior to and during flare activity, with rotational movement accelerating due to shear stresses. This acceleration was likely a result of the region's rapid rotation. Our study offers supporting evidence for the 'toppling' model, which proposes that sunspots remain connected to the underlying layers of the sun's atmosphere until they break free from the disk. Furthermore, these results hold implications for other rotating sunspot observations, particularly those involving NOAA AR 1206, which also showed connected magnetic elements despite rotating off the disk. This supports the idea that magnetic connections remain intact even as sunspots rotate. Based on these findings, the likelihood of magnetic connections remaining intact for other rotating sunspots appears high. Data from the HMI instrument on board the Kepler satellite allowed for confirmation of our observations, yielding detailed maps of the sunspots' movements and magnetic changes. Mumford in 1969. Recent breakthroughs by Edidin-Gentili-Weng and Edidin-Weng, combined with the field-of-jacobs technique established by the lecturer, have made it possible to prove the Mumford Conjecture for numerous cases across different dimensions and degrees. In computational mechanics research, solving cardiac mechanics involves modeling the heart's tissue using highly irregular meshes, especially when using detailed patient-specific imaging data. Due to these complex meshes, the system equations become non-linear, necessitating iterative solution methods that can take advantage of modern computer architectures with thousands of cores. The development of efficient, flexible, and scalable algorithms is crucial for exploiting such computational resources. Three multilevel preconditioners - Balanced Domain Decomposition by means of Algebraic Multigrid, Hierarchical Neumann-Dirichlet and FETI(UG) methods - are implemented and compared in the context of non-linear cardiac mechanics, especially when using highly irregular meshes. The analysis involves presenting new SMAL algorithms for Cardiac Mechanics and an in-depth examination of the implementation details. The study also showcases the performance variability of different SMAL components, emphasizing the importance of algorithmic flexibility, also illustrated by an analysis of solution strategies for Cardiac Mechanics. The analysis ultimately reveals that the Hierarchical Neumann-Dirichlet method exhibits the best performance in a variety of practical scenarios, while the Balanced Domain Decomposition by means of Algebraic Multigrid algorithm performs best when additional memory is available to improve convergence speed. The research makes these multilevel preconditioners available to the public through the GitLab repository \href{https://itc4me.gitlab.io/smal-cardiac/}{itc4me.gitlab.io/smal-cardiac}}. The ever-growing influence of user-generated content is significantly altering the digital landscape, driven in part by the proliferation of systems known as collaborative knowledge-based tagging systems that facilitate user interaction. To better comprehend these systems, we conducted an in-depth study of user engagement patterns within such systems, focusing on task reuse, information exchange, and collaborative activities within a dataset comprising over 958 tasks executed by 120 users across multiple domains. Our analysis reveals that user engagement with these systems adheres to a predictable pattern driven by initial interest, followed by periods of reduced engagement before experiencing a resurgence as the content generated during previous interactions is revisited and built upon. Through our examination of user interactions, we identified various phases of engagement and found that users tend to exhibit shared interests within distinct groups, while also displaying individual preferences and collaborative tendencies across different domains. Notably, our study also uncovers a notable phenomenon where users demonstrate a collective ability to anticipate and respond to each other's queries before they are even posed, highlighting the capacity of these systems to foster a collective intuitive understanding among users. Our findings shed new light on user engagement patterns within collaborative tagging systems, while also paving the way for the development of theoretical frameworks and practical methodologies aimed at optimizing these systems and further leveraging their potential. Recently, two-dimensional acoustic gratings have shown promising results, 
with advancements in theory and experimental proof-of-concepts that match 
theoretical projections. Our research builds upon these findings by taking 
microacoustic technology to the next level, where tiny features affect sound 
waves at ultra-high frequencies, typically in the hundreds of MHz. We design 
a nanoscale mesh that filters sound waves at 550MHz, using a unique "honey-
comb" pattern, constructed from 550MHz resonator cells, using two-photon polymerization. This mesh filters out regular wave patterns while allowing 
encoded information to be transmitted as encrypted pulses, demonstrating the 
potential for secure communication. Additionally, we outline potential uses 
beyond communication, including red-blue coloring and acoustic filtering. This 
work not only pushes the boundaries of acoustic technology but also sets the 
stage for integrating microacoustics into everyday life. \copyright 2023 The

This paper primarily focuses on the long-term behavior of strong solutions to the two-dimensional compressible FENE ribbon model. Utilizing the Fourier splitting technique, we demonstrate that the solutions' time decay rates are capped by certain exponential inequalities. Furthermore, in a low-temperature environment, the solutions converge toward equilibrium by showing the uniform boundedness of the solutions' time derivatives. Consequently, the solutions themselves become uniformly bounded, enabling us to identify the unique, absolutely continuous probability measure, which the solutions converge toward. In a high-temperature setting, the solutions do not converge toward a specific limit; however, the solutions remain uniformly bounded. Nonetheless, by extracting a convergent subsequence, we demonstrate that the limit of the solutions' trajectory is a unique, smooth solution to the same system within the space of integrable functions. In both temperature scenarios, the main tool employed is the Fourier splitting technique. This method not only facilitates the analysis of the solutions' time behavior but also allows us to derive precise estimates of the solutions' time decay rates. In particular, the solutions can be shown to decay at a rate proportional to $t^{-\frac{5}{2}}$ in a low-temperature environment and at a rate proportional to $t^{-\frac{7}{2}}$ in a high-temperature environment. In both cases, the solutions can be shown to decay at a faster rate than those of the 2-D incompressible FENE ribbon model. Additionally, this paper contains an appendix containing an alternative proof of the uniform boundedness of the solutions using the Littlewood-Paley theory and the Besov space. This alternative approach leverages the Fourier splitting technique's analytical merits to derive new inequalities to prove the solutions' uniform boundedness. In doing so, the solutions can be shown to decay at a rate proportional to $t^{-\frac{4}{3}}$ in a low-temperature environment and at a rate proportional to $t^{-\frac{4}{2}}$ in a high-temperature environment. The key steps involved express certain Besov space norms in terms of Littlewood-Paley pieces and the low-frequency component of the solutions, followed by applying Leray's projective limit to derive the necessary inequalities. This approach not only provides insight into the time decay rates but also offers a distinct analytical merit to the long-term behavior of the solutions. Implementing integrated access and backhaul (IAB) through millimeter wave (mmWave) technology holds great promise for delivering fast data to a high density of mobile devices in crowded areas like cities. This approach allows for the coexistence of both fixed and mobile broadband services by enabling the provision of both access and backhaul connections on the same frequency band. However, efficiently deploying IAB mmWave networks in areas with high mobile traffic demands poses significant technical difficulties. In this paper, we delve into the primary problems associated with mobile IAB networks, such as determining the most effective mmWave band utilization methods and deploying network functions effectively. We examine relevant solutions, including the use of mobile backhaul technologies and network optimization techniques. Additionally, we analyze the challenges involved in implementing IAB networks and outline areas for further research, focusing on areas such as mobile video traffic management, network security, and the implementation of intelligent management systems tailored to mobile IAB networks. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the key issues, proposed solutions, and potential challenges associated with implementing mobile IAB networks. It aims to contribute to the development of innovative solutions and provide a framework for further research in this field. Finally, we highlight some exciting and promising areas for future investigation and implementation. This study is expected to pave the way towards a practical implementation of mobile IAB networks. In this study, we conduct an extensive examination of how various methods of establishing the parameters of evolutionary algorithms compare, with a focus on their effectiveness. By employing three different approaches to set the parameters of these algorithms, namely a random, an informative method based on past data, and a informed method based on past data but taking into account how changing the parameters affects the results, we aim to understand which of these strategies is most effective. Our analysis, performed using global sensitivity analysis on three optimization problems with different characteristics, reveals that the informed method based on how changing the parameters affects the results tends to produce better outcomes than the other two approaches, with significant improvements in some cases. Moreover, we found that our sensitivity analysis to be a reliable tool for evaluating the effectiveness of different parameter setting methods. Based on our results, we suggest future researchers to investigate how different ways of setting the parameters setting affect the results and consider using sensitivity analysis to compare their findings with existing results. Additionally, we released the code used in this study to help other researchers repeat our investigation and potentially improve the effectiveness of evolutionary algorithms. Our results could also be seen as a form of transfer learning, where past investigations are used to predict and improve the results of new experiments. Our study has several limitations, notably not conducting a full comparison of the different parameter setting methods to establish a general preference, due to the high computational cost required to do so, and assuming a uniform distribution of the parameters, which may not accurately reflect real-world scenarios. Our results could be extended by applying sensitivity analysis to the results of optimization tasks, rather than just how the parameters affect the results. Our study has several potential applications, including automatically adjusting the parameters of evolutionary algorithms to best fit the characteristics of the problem being optimized and investigating how the parameters of these algorithms contribute to their effectiveness. The interpretation of quantum wave functions remains contentious, particularly regarding their use in determining probability densities. This text seeks to mitigate interpretation issues by offering arguments that support the wave formula for finding energy probabilities. Initially, we examine context-dependent inferences that rely on distance-based measures of similarity between wave functions, which provide a plausible case. Additionally, consider a hypothetical experiment where two particles exhibits entangled energy changes; we investigate the probability of each particle exhibiting a certain energy level, and find that outcomes are indeed doubly exclusive, as required by the wave formula's prediction. A discussion on the range of valid interpretations follows, concluding that our analysis supports an ontologically real view of quantum states. Notably, this view is consistent with the Born statistical account of measuring energy probabilities. This text presents new evidence in favor of the wave formula's reliability in determining probability densities. This reliability, in turn, makes a strong case for an ontologically real interpretation of quantum wave functions. This real view is then shown to be compatible with the statistical approach of Born, particularly when analyzing energy probability distributions. Long-lasting reinforcement learning environments pose challenges to traditional evaluation methods, prompting a need for special settings. In response, research has introduced numerous artificial settings with established rules and goals to enable standard evaluation procedures. Nevertheless, existing settings often require specific expertise or natural scenes to be translated into code, hindering widespread adoption. Moreover, most existing settings rely on random environments that may not adequately mirror real-world scenarios. This paper introduces a new framework, called L2Explorer, which enables the evaluation of ongoing reinforcement learning methods in diverse settings, including both controlled and real-world environments. Based on a study of 12 real-world problems, we examine the ease of configuring artificial environments using our tool and the characteristics of genuine tasks. Unlike other evaluation methods, L2Explorer successfully incorporates real-world challenges in its artificial settings and offers customizable parameters to suit various research objectives. As a result, research teams can employ L2Explorer to assess the performance of their lifelong reinforcement learning methods in artificial and real-world contexts. Meanwhile, a challenge competition has been launched on GitHub to gather more robust benchmarks and drive further improvement in related technologies. Specifically, you can find the code at: https://github.com/jb-mlpr/l2explorer. A web-based interface at lifelong-rl.org also provides access to L2Explorer's documentation, training data, and evaluation results from participating agents. Additionally, the code for our study, including real-world data, is available at: https://github.com/jb-mlpr/evaluation_of_lrl. This includes the repository containing real-world data: https://github.com/jb-mlpr/real_world_data. This paper presents a new standardised approach to evaluate the performance of lifelong reinforcement learning methods. A associated thread on our learning forum can be found at: https://forum.limited.com/topic/21. The full code needed to reproduce our study can be found at: https://github.com/jb-mlpr/associated_code. This includes the code for our artificial settings: https://github.com/jb-mlpr/artificial_settings, the code for our real-world data, including training data: https://github.com/jb-mlpr/real_world_data. This study uncovers a broad class of wave-like disturbances that arise in the short-term dynamics of the two-dimensional Euler equation with smooth initial data that differ from Couette flow. These disturbances maintain their amplitude over time while their position advances at a nonlinear rate determined by their vorticity distribution. Notably, these disturbances can occur even when the initial data vary slowly across one dimension, and their movement is facilitated by areas with high positive vorticity. The authors also demonstrate that these disturbances can propagate to an unlimited distance from the source, ultimately reaching the farthest point of the domain and causing disturbances that persist in the long term. In particular, these wave-like disturbances can emerge in the two-dimensional Euler equation even when the initial data is closely aligned with Couette flow, provided there exists at least one area with minor irregularities in the velocity field. These results can be extended to certain types of quasilinear hyperbolic systems, and the authors also provide analytical evidence that these wave-like disturbances have real-world counterparts in areas such as geophysics and high-energy particle physics. Furthermore, these wave-like disturbances can be observed in both rotating and non-rotating systems. However, when the initial data is closely aligned with Couette flow and features minimal irregularities, these wave-like disturbances can be resolved by current computational methods, and their movement can be accurately predicted using established integration techniques. Nonetheless, as the magnitude of the irregularities increases, these wave-like disturbances become increasingly difficult to track using these methods, and their behavior becomes increasingly difficult to model. Ultimately, these wave-like disturbances and their impacts may hold key implications for understanding and modeling complex phenomena such as geophysical currents and the behavior of charged particles. Moreover, these wave-like disturbances can be observed across various scales, and their movement may leave behind visible marks such as the patterns seen on water surfaces. In summary, these wave-like disturbances represent a previously unappreciated aspect of fluid dynamics and Euler dynamics, and their behavior may not be captured by simplified models such as the Navier-Stokes equation. We introduce a technique for all-optical control of linear polarization within exciton-polariton condensates, employing a microcavity containing two closely spaced quantum wells with randomly aligned transition dipoles. By shifting the beam's polarization, we can trigger transitions between two distinct modes, namely the scissors mode and a mode characterized by a mixed polarization. Our experimental findings demonstrate a high degree of control over the condensate's polarization properties, coupled with efficient coupling between modes. Additionally, we have observed a distinct hysteresis in the system's steady-state polarization, which can be effectively managed through optical input. The problem of determining a boundary's inner location in a 1D scattering problem is addressed through the inverse spectral analysis of transmission eigenfunctions. Essential tools in solving this problem are new formulas for calculating Wronskian values, which enable the selection of specific wave functions at both the interior and exterior regions based on their behavior near the boundary. Utilizing these wave functions, an iterative method is developed to approximate the boundary's inner location. The proposed method's effectiveness is demonstrated through numerical examples. Additionally, considering that phase functions may vanish or become singular, specialized handling is required, and an inner iteration method is proposed to handle such situations effectively. The proposed methods can be extended to address multi-dimensional scattering problems, and specific details for the 2D and 3D cases are provided in the provided supplementary information. However, due to space constraints, these additional details are not included in the current manuscript. As a result, finding the transmission eigenvalues becomes unnecessary, and the proposed methods can be directly applied to calculate the scattering length, a crucial factor in understanding quantum waves' behavior and geophysical fluid dynamics. The methods' applicability and correctness are verified by their successful application in geophysical models as demonstrated in the provided supplementary information. Based on these observations, the proposed methods can be regarded as useful for identifying boundaries and calculating transmission eigenfunctions simultaneously. The provided code can be accessed at the following link: https://github.com/lzhypt/Inneriteration_Te. Our research assesses whether quantum fluctuations occurring during an inflationary period could give rise to primordial black holes (PBHs) that subsequently decay into high-energy particles when they evaporate. It's hypothesized that these particles could be responsible for the origin of ultra-high energy cosmic rays. To investigate this possibility, we first identify the fraction of matter that could give rise to PBHs, and find that this fraction must not exceed $10^{-3}$ if we consider fluctuations in density, due to stability requirements. A similar constraint applies to fluctuations in the primordial magnetic field. However, if the fluctuations in the field lead to localized matter concentrations, a significantly higher fraction of matter can give rise to PBHs, and these more massive black holes can decay into higher-energy particles, producing a broader spectrum of cosmic rays that extends to higher energies. Although our analysis indicates that the radiation from PBH decay is not sufficient to explain the observed pulse in the spectrum of high-energy particles at approximately 99 TeV, our findings also demonstrate that a greater density of PBHs could result in a more substantial radiation output capable of partially accounting for the observed pulse at higher energies. Conversely, a more localized spectrum of high-energy particles is likely to be produced by the decay of a greater density of lighter PBHs. This research highlights potential avenues for further exploration, and encourages a more detailed examination of inflationary perturbations and PBH stability, particularly in light of emerging constraints on dark matter, such as those derived from galaxy rotation curves and Lyman-alpha forest data. Moreover, since the space-time continuum of evaporating PBHs is described by a quantum state characterized by a wave function, this research also stimulates a more fundamental inquiry about the nature of quantum black holes, and whether it is feasible to ascribe a non-trivial wave function to a black hole that continues to evaporate, even when considering the'semi-classical' approximation of quantum theory.
