In the context of digital geometry, we focus on digital planar spanners, specifically those that approximate Euclidean distances with certain bounds. A suitable metric for measuring these distances is provided by L1-approximating geometry, which is closely related to a grid-based structure called digital planar geometry. Our investigations result in the construction of digital Euclidean spanners, which are essentially geometric sketches where nearby points remain close to each other. We demonstrate the existence of efficient, digitized (k, L1)-spanners for all k, which guarantee that the distance between two points remains less than L1 times the original Euclidean distance with a multiplier that approaches 2k+1 as the dimension approaches infinity. We also show that this ratio cannot be less than 2k+1 for general (k, L2)-spanners, indicating that our digitized approximation is nearly optimal. We further analyze and examine the digitized (k, L1)-spanners for specific values of k, including k = 1 and k = 2, for which we derive upper bounds with multiplier 6 and 10 respectively, and design suitable digitized hedgehog and farthest point spanners. These results are accompanied by a linear-time algorithm to embed a (k, L2)-spanner into L1-geometry, which leads to a 2k-1 multiplicative approximation factor for the distance. We demonstrate the existence of a certain type of digitized (2, L1)-spanner with an additive rather than multiplicative distance approximation, which guarantees that adjacent points remain within a certain distance of each other. These results are likely to be of independent interest due to their unique nature. Furthermore, we show that for any point set, a (k, L2)-spanner can be transformed into a digitized geometry with distances that approximate the original Euclidean distances with a certain bound, which is closely related to a certain theoretical geometry known as C-geometry. This led to a new proof of a long-standing conjecture stating that a (2, L2)-spanner can be transformed into a certain digitized geometry, which is known as D-geometry. This digitized geometry can be computed in near-linear time. We also analyzed and examined the properties of a certain geometry known as its "shallow digitized counterpart", which is a certain digitized geometry computed from the original point set's L2-geometry, which in turn can be computed in linear time, for a dimension of at most 4. This study tackles the critical issue of energy efficiency in machine learning model development by targeting feature extraction. During training, the standard approach is to utilize all gathered data features irrespective of their relevance, resulting in heightened energy demands and ineffective data utilization. To optimize this, our proposed framework addresses feature selection and model optimization concurrently, using an innovative two-phase process. Initially, a feature selection method is implemented using a modified version of mutual information, considering data availability and device memory constraints in IoT contexts. Subsequently, the selected features are fed into a lightweight, energy-efficient classifier optimized using an evolutionary balance between accuracy and computational cost. The proposed approach is evaluated through experiments involving synthetic data, comparing it favorably to established state-of-the-art methods in feature selection and model optimization. Notably, our study shows that using the proposed feature selection method with a balanced optimizer yields improved accuracy while significantly reducing energy consumption and computation overhead compared to using all available features. Specifically, the experiments demonstrate reduced energy consumption of up to 68.89% and computation overhead reduction of up to 111.11%, achieved with only a 0.56% decrease in classification accuracy. The selected models produced by our approach remain compact, consisting of no more than three layers with a total of nine neurons. The proposed solution exhibits exceptional practical value for real-world IoT device classification scenarios due to its lightweight, cost-effective, and energy-efficient design. Godel modal logics can be regarded as an extension of basic Godel logic with the consideration of modal operators. To characterise Godel modal logics through algebraic and relational structures, various frameworks have been proposed, but they often fail to cover all cases. This study introduces new algebraic and relational structures to provide a complete characterisation of Godel modal logics. These new structures build upon the established Godel algebras by incorporating modal operators, and are based on the concept of Godel algebras with partial orders. To validate these new structures, respective preservation theorems are demonstrated, and it is proven that they are both unique and sufficient. This study also extends the developed techniques to cover Godel logics with connections, Godel multiplicative modal logics, and other extensions. Additionally, soundness and completeness theorems for these new structures are established, and it is proven that they are equivalent to the existing canonical models. This study introduces canonical Godel modal algebras as the algebraic counterpart to canonical models, and provides a new method to determine the algebraicity of the Godel modal logic formulas. This method relies on the use of Priestley spaces, and leads to a deeper understanding of the extended Godel modal logics. Finally, some notable results on the decidability, complexity, and countability of Godel modal logics are recalled. This study concludes by examining decision procedures for Godel modal logics, and reviewing the established algorithms. Additionally, some open issues and topics for further research are outlined. This study provides a new framework to study finite Godel modal logics through their corresponding modal algebras, and sheds light on the complexity of their decision procedures. This study can be regarded as an extension to the researcher's earlier work on basic Godel logic. This study is organised into two distinct modules. Module I focuses on the development of new algebraic and relational structures to characterise Godel modal logics through their respective algebraic and relational models. This module examines decision procedures for Godel modal logics, and provides a new framework to study finite Godel modal logics through their corresponding modal algebras. Module II focuses on the application and extension of the developed techniques to cover Godel logics with connections, Godel multiplicative modal logics, and other extensions. This module introduces canonical Godel modal algebras as the algebraic counterpart to canonical models, and provides a new method to determine the algebraicity of the Godel modal logic formulas. We suggest an iterative algorithm, distorted resolvent algorithm (DRA), to compute Nash equilibria in various games. This DRA method can be applied to any monotone and $\omega$-regular operators, making it versatile and applicable to a broad range of games. Notably, we provide specific implementations of DRA for finite and infinite repeated games based on dynamic programming. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of distorted resolvent for $\omega$-regular operators, whose continuous inverse generates Nash equilibria in one-shot games. Moreover, we demonstrate that under certain conditions, Nash equilibria in finite repeated games can be computed using the distorted resolvent algorithm. Finally, we supplement our theoretical findings with simple experimental results, showcasing the efficiency of our algorithm in computing Nash equilibria for finite repeated games. However, we also encounter difficulties in directly applying our method to infinite repeated games and suggest future research in this area. Additionally, we assume knowledge of the necessary background in $\omega$-regular operators and online learning.

We conducted research into a system at equilibrium that features large polyhedra made up of several spherical cores, using Monte Carlo simulation to explore its properties. These polyhedra have vertices connected by rigid, equal-length bonds that allow for continuous rotation. To enhance simulation efficiency, we developed an efficient move type that works well within the reference frame in which the system's internal structure is defined. This move involves rotating a selected particle by a random angle relative to its neighboring particles. Our simulations revealed that, under certain conditions, the system enters a phase characterized by wavy formations. These formations straighten out when the system is stimulated to adopt more closed shapes. When the system is stimulated to adopt more open shapes, it enters another phase characterized by random movements. We observed that the formations change with variations in the number of spherical cores these polyhedra consist of. Specifically, when these polyhedra consist of fewer than eight spherical cores, they cannot form a full cube due to lack of sufficient rigidity to maintain a stable solid structure. However, when they consist of eight or more spherical cores, they gain enough rigidity to maintain a stable solid structure and enter a phase characterized by close packing. When the system is stimulated to adopt more open shapes, it enters another phase characterized by random movements. Additionally, when these polyhedra consist of an odd number of spherical cores and sufficient interparticle interactions are present, they enter a phase characterized by random movements. We recorded and documented all these observations in a series of pressure-density phase diagrams we constructed. These phase diagrams offer a valuable comparison with existing theories and experiments on systems composed of hard polyhedra. They also reveal previously unreported phenomena. Moreover, they confirm some of these theories and make accurate predictions for other systems composed of hard polyhedra. Finally, these phase diagrams could provide essential guidance in applications such as liquid crystal technology and colloidal science. They offer a useful comparison between theory and experiment and provide essential input for simulations of systems composed of hard polyhedra. We also note that, although we observed some similarities with liquid crystal materials composed of tapering rods, we did not replicate the entire behavior reported in the literature for these materials. However, we did successfully replicate some of the transitions and phases characterized by random movements that are also commonly found in other systems composed of hard polyhedra. Additionally, we noted that the system is always in a state of internal equilibrium that is independent of the reference frame in which the system is observed. The nature of friction at a liquid foam interface has historically been considered either completely liquid-like or completely solid-like in its behavior, with recent studies through the analysis of soap film friction even categorizing it as quantum-like. This study, focusing on a weaker version of this theory, employs a friction law rooted in nanoscale surface irregularities rather than intermolecular forces, conducts an experiment to verify this hypothesis by comparing frictional behavior under different conditions. This is done while taking into account that the existing quantum-based model does not account for the effects seen in this study that relate the way a liquid flows to the size of the liquid's bubbles. Consequently, the existing quantum-based model does not adequately explain the observed effects, suggesting the need for an alternative model that can better account for surface structure and the distribution of viscoelastic stresses. Ultimately, the study finds support for a friction model that incorporates aspects of micro-jets and droplets. This model considers the impacts of surface structure and the resulting stresses that arise due to the viscoelastic properties of the liquids involved. This study presents a new perspective that can help understand and study friction at a liquid foam interface, providing a potential foundation for the development of a more detailed model that can bridge the gap between microscopic and macroscopic physics. This model has the potential to apply to various materials beyond just liquid foams by addressing a long-standing question regarding the nature of friction. Additionally, this study introduces a new method that allows for the elimination of surface structure effects, allowing for a more in-depth analysis of the liquid's viscoelastic properties. This proof involves a straightforward construction and avoids the use of modulated Sobolev spaces, as contrasted with earlier studies on this topic. Introduction of a new variable and a specific energy-type inequality serve as the core elements of this proof. This method of construction is reminiscent of a technique first suggested by Bourgain and Choen in a different context. Essentially, our argument demonstrates that a particular nonlinear operation results in an unbounded output when applied to certain classes of smooth vector fields with specified growth rates, which in turn leads to the instability of the equations in question. This argument can be extended to various types of solutions, including those with initial conditions and time-dependent data. This proof not only provides a straightforward approach to establishing the instability of Euler equations at a threshold in Sobolev spaces but also reveals an interesting property of a particular Lorentz space with a very low decay rate. This proof does not utilize any form of compactness or structural decomposition and directly constructs an example that grows exponentially without bound, which in turn makes the solutions exhibit the characteristics of ill-posedness. This study introduces a novel image concealment technique, reversible concealment, which seamlessly restores original images from masked versions with minimal perturbations during the masking process. We devise a constructive method for implementing reversible concealment functions using Bayesian Neural Networks, enabling us to derive original images from masked versions with minimal adjustments. By initializing BNNs with suitable priors, we achieve low frequency adjustments during the masking process and develop an efficient way to train BNNs, leading to the development of an end-to-end training method for our constructive approach. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through comparative experiments on widely-used benchmark datasets. Additionally, we showcase the applicability of our method to the creation of stealthy adversarial examples. Further details are available in the supplementary material. The code for this project can be accessed at https://github.com/jbarez/Reversible-Concealment-BNN. \\

High-resolution observations of the solar photosphere reveal tiny magnetic bright points, associated with extremely short-lived events (SSLERs) that indicate intense magnetic fields. These SSLERs are significantly brighter than quiet regions and vary in duration from 18 to 42 seconds. Analysis of time series data captured by the G-band filtergraph instrument on the Big Bear 16-inch telescope demonstrates that SSLERs can be described by a bi-modal distribution, corresponding to longer and shorter events. These two-part distributions are compared to the empirical power law, showing that SSLERs follow a bi-powery law with varying exponents, indicating a common origin for SSLERs of all lengths. Breakdown of the data into periods of high and low activity reveals that the bi-powery distributions vary accordingly, as well as with solar cycle phase and latitude. These findings are consistent with a theoretical understanding of magnetic bright points, suggesting that they are a primary indicator of the intense magnetic fields that drive solar eruptions and other complex behaviors. Further investigation is necessary to determine the precise relationship between these events and the magnetic fields that fuel them. Minimal films are an ongoing research area in human vision, encompassing several theoretical aspects. This study focuses on understanding how humans extract movement information to recognize objects, using experiments that compared human responses to videos created using two different methods: one optimally extracting essential movement data and another introducing random movements to aid object recognition. These trials examined how humans perceive 3D shapes from moving textures and the combined effect of these shapes and textures. Notably, humans struggled to recognize objects in videos featuring multiple moving textures, outperforming a machine learning model only when the videos contained clear shapes to guide the recognition process. Additionally, humans demonstrated the ability to distinguish between intricate 3D shapes based on movement cues, but this capability faded when the shapes were overly complex and difficult to extract essential movement information from. This study's findings contradict a widely held hypothesis suggesting humans rely on overall movement patterns to recognize objects, instead indicating that humans can efficiently extract essential movement data using minimal computational resources. Finally, we analyzed videos collected through a previous study and found that humans can efficiently extract movement information, resulting in a novel dataset and a machine learning model that can be reconfigured to match human performance, offering potential applications in both biological and artificial motion analysis. Overall, this study brings together existing research on minimal films, movement extraction, and shape recognition to shed new light on the underlying mechanisms of human dynamic object recognition. It also introduces an innovative approach to movement analysis, utilizing active experimentation to refine a previously proposed theory. Furthermore, we identified an unexpected aspect of human movement processing and provided a versatile model that can be reconfigured to mimic human behavior, having practical implications for dynamic scene understanding. Lastly, we proposed an objective evaluation method to gauge the plausibility of artificial models mimicking human motion perception. We show that the first eigenvalue of a second-order, nonlinear elliptic operator with power-type nonlinearities and bounded Robin boundary conditions can be approximated with precision by a linearized eigenvalue of another elliptic operator, specifically one with a nonlinear source term and Robin boundary conditions. This approximation is precise in the sense that the error remains uniform as the parameter goes to zero. Moreover, this result has implications for the homogenization of a related problem involving a nonlinear elliptic operator with periodic inclusions and internal phonomena. Specifically, we find that the (formal) spectral problem of this heterogenous medium is equivalent to the limit of a family of spectral problems of homogeneous media with a nonlinear source term, all with a common Robin boundary condition. This generalizes a previous result of our own and presents novel behavior. Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) have gained prominence in handling irregular data structures, albeit with some researchers expressing skepticism over the theoretical underpinnings of GCNNs. The process of graph convolution involves a complex interplay between node features and spatial relationships, making it difficult to grasp intuitively. We propose a novel perspective on GCNNs, basing them on a straightforward idea - that of matched filtering, where node features undergo a weighted transformation based on neighbor influences. This simplified framework demonstrates how node features evolve as you move through the graph, ultimately revealing the justification for the graph convolution operation. The analysis also sheds light on challenges like Scattering Transform limitations and the circular down-sampling nature of graph Fourier transform, ultimately making GCNNs accessible to a broader machine learning community. The study further explores the compatibility of GCNNs with frequency domain representations, exemplified by our analysis of the graph Hadamard transform. The findings are further substantiated by our empirical investigation of GCNNs applied to node classification on three well-known benchmark datasets - ChestX-ray, Fundus, and PASCAL-VOC 2012 - where we compared standard graph convolution against our theoretically-motivated filter matching GCNN and the existing state-of-the-art MixHop. The study shows that the latter two outperform the former and often surpass other leading methods on these datasets, largely due to its capability of exploiting crucial spatial relationships within images, thereby generating robust multi-hop graph representations. The study makes these findings accessible through an interactive Jupyter notebook, enabling others to replicate the experiments and learn about the training process of GCNNs. Currently, Choiceless Polynomial Time (CPT) stands out as the most promising approach to tackle decision problems within PTIME (polynomial time) complexity class, having demonstrated the ability to logically encapsulate numerous PTIME decision problems, as well as essential PTIME hybrid tumbling block and nested view block operators used in prior research. Building upon this foundation, a new specification technique is proposed for CPT, enabling the determination of a circuit's computational property utilizing its input and output symmetric characteristics. This leads to a crucial discovery: any CPT-based graph property can be effectively captured through a complementary graph's symmetric circuit, ultimately resulting in CPT's capability to address the parity graph property, previously unaddressed. As a consequence, CPT can now encompass the linear programming feasibility problem, marking a significant departure from its earlier distinction between feasible and infeasible problems. This breakthrough also brings CPT closer to the monotone hybrid tumbling block operator, used earlier in Vector Logic, as well as solidifies its solid feasibility-based foundation. CPT can predominantly be defined through polynomial-sized complementary circuits, except in specific cases requiring exhaustive examination of all n variables, particularly as it applies to co-COL and Minimum Linear Program (MLP) feasibility problems. MLP feasibility, an integral part of linear programming, falls under the domain of co-COL, prompting the need to examine all n variables to determine if a particular linear program has a feasible solution. This fundamental change presents CPT with a possibility of hierarchically expanding its own bounds by incorporating variable quantities of extra "hiding" view blocks, potentially encompassing even parity on general graphs as a decision problem within a expanded CPT framework. As a result, CPT now stands at the threshold of encompassing a significant portion of the PTIME complexity class, notably including crucial decision problems like Graph Isomorphism and within a expanded CPT framework, even parity on general graphs. Historically significant paradigms like Polynomial Time and NP have been encompassed by newer approaches such as Fixed Point Logic and CPT, suggesting that these more expressive approaches may continue to encompass established ones. CPT, in its current form, primarily captures a distinct property of symmetric circuits, although it can effectively describe hybrid tumbling block and nested view block operators used previously in Vector Logic. This improvement is achieved through a loop consisting of prediction, refinement, and propagation. However, the original BasicVSR's reliance on a single module for frame prediction and reliance on an auxiliary scale propagation network has created limitations in its ability to learn relevant features. Furthermore, its reliance on a coarse-to-fine scaling scheme, which requires interpolating missing frames, can introduce downscaling artifacts. To address these issues, a new approach, BasicVSR++, has been developed. This improvement involves leveraging a self-attention based frame prediction module and incorporating a bidirectional temporal propagation scheme that directly scales video frames without intermediate interpolations. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of BasicVSR++ over the previous approach and showcase its state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmark datasets. Additionally, BasicVSR++ has been found to be efficient and adaptable, achieving impressive results even in resource-constrained scenarios. Its success in video enhancement tasks serves as a new standard for future research in VSR. The code for BasicVSR++ is openly available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/IngraoClement/BasicVSR++.py. BasicVSR++ has been officially released on MMEditing: https://mmediting.github.io/BasicVSR++_docs/index.html. In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that
employing a single shared dynamics model actually increases the likelihood of
information overload and catastrophic training interference in tasks requiring
distinct world environments. Consequently, we propose the Modular Networks for
Multi-task Reinforcement Learning (MUMRL) method, which utilizes an individual
dynamics model for each individual task to effectively learn a variety of
tasks. On top of that, we also introduce a novel offline RL benchmark called
Gridworld MTB, alongside a set of repeatable training-testing scenarios that
can be scaled up to accommodate growing numbers of tasks. Overall, our study
highlights the potential drawbacks of using a shared representation in model-based
multi-task reinforcement learning settings and introduces a simple yet effective
solution. Moreover, our contribution also includes a set of benchmark suites
called MTB that can be utilized by the community to advance the state of the art
in model-based multi-task reinforcement learning settings. This benchmark suite
includes a variety of training-testing scenarios that can be scaled up to
accommodate growing numbers of tasks. Specifically, it includes a benchmark
suite called Gridworld MTB that consists of repeatable training-testing scenarios
at varying scales of 2, 4, 8, and 16 tasks. Additionally, it also includes
another benchmark suite called Mountain Car MTB that consists of a single task
with 4 variants of additional rewards. While it may also be utilized to advance
the state of the art in model-based reinforcement learning settings, its suite
consists of relatively small-scale training-info and can be considered as
difficult to scale up due to its strong data-locality. Our study employs
population-based training, which includes a variety of techniques such as
evolutionary strategies, neural structured statics, and reinforcement search to
evaluate the performance of model-based multi-task reinforcement learning
settings by comparing them against a variety of baseline methods. Our study
boasts of self-normalizing properties as our training dynamics models are
constructed independently for each individual task without any shared
representation. Consequently, it does not suffer from information overload and
catastrophic training interference as explicitly mentioned in its main
contributions

We've developed a strategy to maximize the work extracted during a finite time interval, subject to a restriction on the rate of heat transfer and initial/final system state. Our approach involves converting this problem into a quadratic optimization issue, which yields relevant thermodynamic properties as functions of time. This research introduces a spatially-resolved model for analyzing the effect of hurricanes and storm surges on power systems. Previous studies primarily focused on the impact of hurricanes as a whole, without considering the storm surge that can severely damage infrastructure in low-lying coastal areas. To simulate the spatial reach of the hurricane and storm surge, a geographic information system (GIS) is utilized to expand the map of the power system into a 2D terrain map. The simulated hurricane and storm surge allow for the identification of affected zones, which are then combined with reliability constraints to create an optimization problem. This spatial model is applied to a simplified 69-bus power system and the results show a reduction in total system damage of $44.1 million when considering the storm surge, as opposed to a $20.5 million reduction without taking it into account. Due to the large number of variables and constraints, solving the proposed optimization problem is computationally infeasible through conventional methods; hence, a two-stage optimization approach is proposed to find a computationally-efficient solution. Moreover, a spatial impact analysis is conducted on the power system to determine the relative importance of different load zones. This analysis demonstrates that Zone 10 carries the greatest relative importance in terms of load, which is consistent with its location in the storm's path and low elevation above sea level. This research presents an initial study on analyzing the effect of hurricanes and storm surges on power systems and identifies several areas for further exploration. Some potential areas of future research include incorporating actual hurricane and storm surge data, integrating more detailed system models, and exploring novel optimization algorithms. Additionally, the proposed spatial model can be applied beyond power systems and has potential applications in emergency management, transportation systems, and emergency services. To validate the spatial model and assess its applicability, a case study is conducted on Liberty County, Georgia, utilizing real-world hurricane and storm surge data from Hurricane Irma. This case study demonstrates the ability of the spatial model to replicate actual hurricane and storm surge conditions and identifies vulnerable areas in the county. Furthermore, a comparison is made between the simulated and actual storm conditions, which shows a close match between the two; hence, the spatial model can be utilized for simulated risk assessments and planning purposes. Moreover, the spatial model can aid in determining which areas to prioritize in storm surge mitigation plans and inform decision-making regarding construction projects. As the maps undergo a natural scaling, their foliations either consolidate or fragment, leading to an emergence of non-accessible entropy values. Entropies from pre-image iterations are preserved, while new ones emerge from the map's intrinsic foliation. We compute the scaling-implicit foliation in each iteration, creating a cascade of ergodic measures that are either one-dimensional or two-dimensional. A mechanism for entropy inaccessibility occurs when a tangent trajectory generates a pair of non-converging orbits with the same entropy, thereby blocking entropy increase. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch range issue in WaveNet (WN) through expanded convolution neural network (FCNN) architecture. WN can generate high-fidelity audio signals with considerable pitch ranges; however, its effectiveness heavily relies on the number of training data. Drawing analogies between WN and image prediction, QPNet employs pitch-dependent expanded convolution neural network to mimic the audio generation process, effectively increasing the model's receptive field along the time axis. Experimental results demonstrate that WN combined with FCNN can achieve nearly unsurpassable performance in raw waveform generation. Additionally, our analysis highlights the critical role of WN in basis generation, contributing to the success of the model. Subsequently, we propose to integrate WN and FCNN as Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet), an autonomous generative model capable of generating high-quality audio signals with substantial pitch ranges directly from raw waveforms. Notably, our best model outperformed the current best WaveNet model by 0.16 in the mean opinion scoring. Moreover, QPNet shows superior applicability in voice extension, as evidenced by generated speech samples reaching near-native quality levels. Our model and related code are open-source available at the github.com/zzgao/WaveNet_plus, including raw waveform extension. The effectiveness of collaborative filtering techniques depends largely on finding accurate user-item similarity matrices. Given that user ratings are infrequent, sparse, and subjective, this work investigates how grouping users and items into clusters can enhance prediction accuracy. Unlike existing approaches that treat each group as a whole, our proposed method considers the unique preferences within each cluster. This entails quantifying each user's preferred items on an individual basis, effectively creating an ordinal multi-dimensional rating space for each user. Based on this multi-dimensional representation, we develop a novel bicluster-based collaborative filtering algorithm. This method calculates the likelihood of an unrated item being preferred by a user by analyzing the ranks of corresponding items preferred by that user. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed algorithm outperforms leading collaborative filtering methods, including CF-Gaussian, CF-Linear, CF-NN, CF-LSTM, CF-SVD, CF-NCF, CF-VID, DeepCF, WideCF, and AutoRec. Furthermore, integrating this algorithm with existing methods significantly enhances their predictive capabilities, underscoring its potential as a complementary technique. Implementation details, including the code, are available online for reproduction of our results at https://github.com/khoihuc/UserSpecificBiclusterCf. Detecting Earth-like planets with high precision is hindered by stellar activity. Identifying novel indicators that better reflect a star's magnetic behavior is essential for distinguishing these signals from a planet's Doppler signal. In this research, we analyzed data from the HARPS-N solar telescope project, examining spectral features that change over time on the Sun. These features are affected by sunspots and stellar activity, making it essential to establish a reliable indicator that is not influenced by these variations. We investigated various activity indicators and their connections to features like the solar 5.1 year activity cycle, as well as the characteristics of sunspots. We identified the SII 680.6 nm sunspot index as the most stable indicator and discussed its properties further. Discussion of potential applications to other stars and G stars in particular is also included. Conducting similar observations on other stars using the same method could provide active regions' spectral influence and activity levels, ultimately helping to eliminate variations caused by stellar activity in planetary Doppler signals. This elimination is crucial for accurately detecting other Earths. An open-source code for the analysis is available online at https://github.com/CCU-MOURL/Solar_analysis/tree/master/HARPS-N_SII.1.0.0.

A wide variety of image editing tasks rely on colourisation techniques that were originally developed to add colour to black and white photos. However, these approaches often depend on being able to access the original grayscale image, which isn't always possible in real-world scenarios. Researchers have recently introduced a new framework known as colour transfer, allowing individuals to specify a style pair consisting of colour images rather than individual grayscale pictures. This enables the ability to colour any grayscale image by being given a sample of an image exhibiting the desired colour style. However, existing methods are often slow and produce undesirable distortions in the form of colour spikes. This paper delves into the limitations of these earlier methods, before introducing an innovative approach which uses image residuals to capture a style's characteristics. This style capture approach results in more realistic and efficient results when applied to colour transfer tasks. Furthermore, it also enables the development of an inverse colour transfer method, allowing individuals to derive a colourised image from a style pair, even without access to the original grayscale image. Experiments have demonstrated that the method outperforms existing approaches in a range of quantitative metrics, before being applied in various real-world demonstrations. This technical report showcases the winning model developed for the AQTC challenge within the framework of the LOVEU dataset, which was utilized in the CVPR 2022 conference. The LoveU corpus is an auxiliary dataset created to complement the M2M-PPA training corpus, which was designed to enhance the model's capacity to grasp paragraph-level semantics. The selected dataset comprises Chinese human dialogue as its spoken language and English as the written language. The primary objective of the AQTC challenge revolves around resolving ambiguous pronouns to facilitate seamless switching between spoken and written texts.

The winning model constructed a graph with nodes representing entities and edges with contextually-related weights. A specialized neural network processed entity features to produce a unified vector representation for each entity. The winning model further incorporated a masked object prediction (MOP) objective to refine entity representations by masking a specific object in each sentence and asking the model to predict it. The model was fine-tuned using the AQTC task within the MMD-Zeros framework and achieved impressive results, notably featuring the lowest system-level ambiguity error rate. The report provides a thorough explanation of the winning model and its performance on the LOVEU corpus, including MMD-Zeros training logs, model hyperparameters, and a PyTorch model replica. The report also presents an open investigation into entity representation, proposing an additional comparison with the simple average (SAV) method. The proposed entity representation replicated the performance of the initial winning model and offered enhanced results when fine-tuned, representing a more efficient approach. The proposed replica models are made accessible on the MIT-ML website for easy access. The report finally presents enhanced models, including a BERT-based model and a RoBERTa-based model, which were trained using the same entity representation but with distinct languages, achieving notable results on languages other than Chinese. These models were trained on non-Chinese languages as per the requirements of the AQTC challenge. The proposed models, along with their training logs and PyTorch replicas, are made available on the MIT-ML website, aiming to contribute to the language community, addressing questions, and resolving issues related to the original winning model. The report has been updated to address a critical issue and provide a new solution. The report has been publicly available since July 26, 2021, and the model hyperparameters have been publicly accessible since September 2, 2021. This field research focuses on the settlement of snow particles in atmospheric turbulence. A sophisticated imaging technique is employed to capture the details of snow particle deposition. The analysis reveals a distinct, highly turbulent structure surrounding a settling particle, indicating that the particle's presence modulates the underlying fluid flow. The size and shape of this turbulent region, known as a selective sweeping zone, correlate directly with the particle's diameter. The rate at which snow particles settle is influenced by two key factors: the particle's weight and the intensity of the turbulent motion. A theoretical model is presented to explain this phenomenon, describing how the particle's settling velocity is influenced by the interaction between turbulent eddies and the particle's weight. The model incorporates the concepts of swept areas and swept times, demonstrating that larger particles settle more quickly due to increased swept areas. The model's accuracy is validated using independent measurements and the results agree with previous research findings. The parameters influencing the particle's settling velocity, such as turbulence properties and particle density, can be extracted from the model. The model's applicability extends beyond snow particles to the settlement of other particles, like sediment in water and atmospheric particles. The study's findings could be further explored using numerical models based on the particle's trajectory and the surrounding flow. The research has the potential to be taken up by other scientists and applied in relevant applications. A related investigation can be conducted in a laboratory setting to further refine the study's hypotheses and the theoretical model. The Pacific Lamprey is a parasitic fish that attaches itself to host animals or surfaces coated with a thin layer of mucus, then contracts to create a negative pressure that enables it to move upwards. In contrast to robots using gecko-inspired adhesive force or suction, our solution relies on a simpler, more robust method. We developed a robot capable of mimicking the Pacific Lamprey's adhesive and climbing abilities using just a simple valve and flexible membrane. The valve can create a controlled flow of fluid out of the membrane, resulting in a surface tension that generates an upward force strong enough to overcome gravity. Although the force per unit area produced is relatively low compared to other adhesive robots, our design has several advantages, including a very simple and robust valve-membrane assembly. The robot's climbing ability has been successfully demonstrated in simulated and real environments, with tests conducted in both static and dynamic conditions. Validation experiments, including the analysis of a network involving the interaction of vehicles, air traffic control, and financial transactions, demonstrate the superiority of $ \delta$SAPD over the original SAPD algorithm. I contend that Galileo's methodology was flawed because he relied heavily on experimentation, prioritizing observation over more essential philosophical inquiry. His emphasis on empirical evidence led to a false dichotomy between mathematics and philosophy, causing him to undervalue the latter. Despite his significant scientific contributions, Galileo's true legacy lies in promoting a misguided philosophy that emphasizes experimentation above all else. His influence has persisted through the ages, contaminating the scientific community with a faulty world view that must be confronted. In this account, I seek to reinterpret Galileo's career, highlighting his failures as a philosopher in order to make a broader argument about the nature of inquiry. Ultimately, I suggest that philosophy plays a vital role in guiding scientific investigation and that a deeper understanding of this role is necessary for a meaningful critique of modern science. By examining Galileo's mistakes, we can distill the essential components of philosophical inquiry and develop a plan to revive and strengthen this essential component of the investigatory process. At its core, this work is a call to action, urging readers to join me in exploring the fundamental questions that underlie all inquiry, including those related to science. In place of a conventional conclusion, I have offered an alternative examination of Galileo's place in the history of thought, one that draws on the insights developed throughout this work. In this addendum, I consider the responses of David Ray Griffin and Alfred Ayer to the arguments presented in the text. In responding to these critics, I have taken the opportunity to refine my position and offer additional clarification, when necessary, on various points. In particular, I have sought to address Griffin's distinction between Galileo's method and that of Einstein, as well as Ayer's criticism of my conception of philosophical inquiry. Furthermore, I have sought to show that this conception is consistent with the views of Plato and Aristotle, even as I have acknowledged significant differences between our respective positions. In reflecting on these differences, I have developed a new appreciation for the enduring power of philosophical ideas. Rather than dismissing these ideas as obsolete, I believe that they retain relevance in the modern era. The analysis of magnetic reconnection, a collisionless process, necessitates complex, computationally intensive kinetic models, contrasting with more feasible fluid-based simulations. Our study utilizes the Magnetohydrodynamics with Adaptable Embedded Particle-in-Cell (MHD-AEPIC) model to investigate the interaction between two magnetic flux ropes. By embedding kinetic models into MHD simulations only in relevant areas, this novel model enables more efficient computation. The comparative study involves three scenarios: the MHD-AEPIC model paired with two distinct electron distribution functions, as well as a fully kinetic approach using the EMHD-PIC model for comparison. The examination of reconnection dynamics, including the formation and coalescence of magnetic islands within these scenarios, is the focus of our investigation. Additionally, we explore the coalescence of multiple islands in the MHD-AEPIC model and highlight its potential to generate complex, non-intuitive reconnection phenomena. Finally, we discuss the comparative results and assess the potential of the MHD-AEPIC model to replicate realistic reconnection scenarios. Its capability to efficiently investigate the coalescence of numerous magnetic islands makes it a promising tool for a broader range of reconnection research. Moreover, its potential to encompass extensively broad parameter spaces adds to its allure as a reconnection model. The studies presented here lay the groundwork for employing the MHD-AEPIC model as an innovative tool for examining reconnection phenomena. It potentially enables the discovery of previously unexamined, core reconnection mechanisms due to its capacity to efficiently investigate a substantially wider range of reconnection scenarios than was previously feasible. As such, this work may contribute to a fresh understanding of the underlying physics of reconnection. In particular, it may offer new insights into the reconnection process at work in astrophysical and laboratory settings. It also has the promise to shed new light on the reconnection process at work in solar system contexts. Specifically, it may contribute to a fresh understanding of the reconnection events at work on the sun and in Earth's magnetosphere. Furthermore, it may offer fresh insights into the reconnection events at play in near-Earth space and the geospace environment. Additionally, it may contribute to a fresh understanding of the reconnection process in laboratory settings found in facilities such as tokamaks and stellarators. In today's fast-paced software development environment, there are numerous tools vying for attention, including an abundance of coding assistants, code review tools, and bug tracking systems. However, many of these tools often remain unconnected, failing to harness their collective potential. To address this issue, we present Amanuensis, a novel concept for an integrated coding companion that leverages a hybrid of human and machine-based intelligence to streamline software development. By drawing on insights from cognitive psychology and software engineering, we've developed a practical approach for implementing Amanuensis, including a trainable component that learns from established research in these fields. Through a practical demonstration, we'll illustrate how Amanuensis, in its initial form, can serve as a valuable resource for junior developers, serving as a developmental guide and mentor until they attain expertise, while also providing a platform for ongoing, naturalistic learning. As such, Amanuensis represents a versatile tool with numerous applications beyond coding training, encompassing various forms of vocational guidance. Experimental evaluation will follow in a companion paper. This PPOI research focuses on understanding how jobs change when tasks are automated. In this project, we're examining the opposite dynamic – how a task affects the job – by looking at coding, a profession impacted by numerous automated tools. As such, Amanuensis serves as both an integrated assistant for coding and a theoretical model for the effects of automation on skilled workers, including developers. While Amanuensis is initially presented as a helpful tool, its characteristics also address core concerns surrounding automation, particularly job displacement. Thus, this work can be seen as a simulation of a task on a job, using coding as a prime example.
